blocks.content: 1. What Is the YAGNI Principle?
blocks.text: 1. What Is the YAGNI Principle?

blocks.content: "Always implement things when you actually need them, never when you just foresee that you need them." Ron Jeffries, co-founder of Extreme Programming
YAGNI is not about writing sloppy code. It is not about ignoring good design. It is about one simple discipline: do not add something until a real requirement demands it.
Every time you catch yourself thinking:
["\"We might need this later\"","\"Let me make this flexible just in case\"","\"What if the requirements change someday\""]
items: "We might need this later"
"Let me make this flexible just in case"
"What if the requirements change someday"

blocks.content: That is YAGNI warning you to stop.
When the need actually arrives, you will have much better information about what to build and how to build it. Building it today based on a guess is almost always wrong.
2. The Real World Problem
blocks.text: 2. The Real World Problem

blocks.content: Let's say you are building a feature for a food delivery app. The requirement is simple. A customer places an order, and the app sends them a confirmation message. That is it.
But then the thinking starts.
What if we need to support email later? Better add a messaging interface. What if we add SMS? Better build a provider system. What if third party services want to plug in? Better create a factory.
So instead of writing a simple notification sender, the developer builds this:
Without YAGNI
blocks.text: Without YAGNI

blocks.content: Step 1: Create an interface for all possible message types
blocks.text: Step 1: Create an interface for all possible message types

blocks.content: Step 2: Create a factory to manage providers
blocks.text: Step 2: Create a factory to manage providers

blocks.content: Step 3: Build an email adapter nobody asked for
blocks.text: Step 3: Build an email adapter nobody asked for

blocks.content: Step 4: Wire everything together in an engine
blocks.text: Step 4: Wire everything together in an engine

blocks.content: The requirement was one thing: send a confirmation message. Instead we now have one interface, one factory, one empty adapter, and one engine. The email adapter has empty method bodies. The factory manages exactly one provider. Nothing here serves any real user.
With YAGNI
blocks.text: With YAGNI

blocks.content: Step 1: Write one simple class that does the job
blocks.text: Step 1: Write one simple class that does the job

blocks.content: Step 2: Use it directly
blocks.text: Step 2: Use it directly

blocks.content:
OrderNotifier notifier = new OrderNotifier();
notifier.sendConfirmation("user123", "2x Burger, 1x Fries");

notifier.sendConfirmation("user123", "2x Burger, 1x Fries");

notifier.sendConfirmation("user123", "2x Burger, 1x Fries");
codes.python:
OrderNotifier notifier = new OrderNotifier();
notifier.sendConfirmation("user123", "2x Burger, 1x Fries");

blocks.content: That is it. Two steps. One class. Zero dead code. It meets today's requirement completely and can be extended the moment a real new requirement arrives.
3. Why Building Too Early Hurts
blocks.text: 3. Why Building Too Early Hurts

blocks.content: Wastes time. Every hour spent on speculative features is an hour not spent on what users actually need today.
Adds confusion. New developers see the factory and the interface and assume there is a reason for all that complexity. They are scared to remove it. Dead code becomes permanent by accident.
Delays real value. The simple version could have been done in an hour. The overengineered version took a day. Users waited longer for something nobody asked for.
Creates hidden maintenance. Even unused code needs updating when dependencies change. Dead code is not free. It is debt that quietly grows.
4. When It Is Okay to Plan Ahead
blocks.text: 4. When It Is Okay to Plan Ahead

blocks.content: YAGNI has exceptions. But they all share one thing in common: the need is real and known, not imagined.
Security and compliance. If the law requires audit logs or encryption from day one, build them. That is not speculation. That is a requirement.
Known long term constraints. If you know from the start the system must handle millions of users, some architectural decisions must be made early. Retrofitting scale is expensive.
Shared libraries. If other teams depend on your code, API design needs more upfront thought. But even then, start minimal and expand based on real usage.
The rule is simple. If you know you need it, build it. If you are just guessing, wait.
5. How YAGNI Reinforces the Overengineering Lesson
blocks.text: 5. How YAGNI Reinforces the Overengineering Lesson

blocks.content: YAGNI and overengineering are the same problem seen from two different angles. Overengineering is the diagnosis, the name for what a codebase looks like after too much speculative structure has been added. YAGNI is the discipline that prevents you from getting there in the first place.
Same Root Cause, Two Names
blocks.text: Same Root Cause, Two Names

blocks.content: Every overengineered interface, factory, or plugin system started as a small decision to build for a future that had not arrived yet. That decision, made once, is a YAGNI violation. Made repeatedly across a codebase, the accumulated result is what the earlier lesson called overengineering. One is the moment, the other is the pattern that emerges when the moment repeats.
YAGNI Is the Daily Discipline, Overengineering Is the Failure Mode
blocks.text: YAGNI Is the Daily Discipline, Overengineering Is the Failure Mode

blocks.content: Think of it as cause and effect. YAGNI is a question you ask yourself before writing a line of code: does a real requirement need this right now? Overengineering is what a codebase looks like when that question was skipped often enough that nobody remembers why the abstraction is there.

blocks.title: Callback to Overengineering vs Good Design
blocks.content: The earlier lesson on overengineering introduced a heuristic before adding an abstraction, and the Rule of Three, which says wait for a third concrete use case before generalizing. Those same checks are YAGNI in practice. If you have not read that lesson yet, the two chapters are meant to be read together, one describes the discipline, the other describes what happens when it slips.
Where They Diverge
blocks.text: Where They Diverge

blocks.content: The distinction worth keeping is scope. YAGNI applies to a single decision, one method, one class, one config option, right now, should this exist. Overengineering describes the accumulated state of a system after many such decisions went the wrong way. You practice YAGNI to avoid ending up with an overengineered system.

A Two Line Test
blocks.text: A Two Line Test

blocks.content: If you can answer both of these honestly, you are almost certainly fine. First, does a real, named requirement need this right now. Second, if I skip it today, is adding it later cheap. If the answer to the first is no and the answer to the second is yes, you are looking at a YAGNI violation waiting to happen.
6. Concrete Signs You Are Violating YAGNI
blocks.text: 6. Concrete Signs You Are Violating YAGNI

blocks.content: Some violations are obvious the day they are written. Most are not. They look reasonable in the moment and only reveal themselves as dead weight once you go looking for them. Here are the ones that show up most often in real codebases.
The Config Option Nobody Has Ever Changed
blocks.text: The Config Option Nobody Has Ever Changed

blocks.content: A settings file has a flag like enableLegacyMode or maxRetryOverride. Check the git blame. It was added two years ago, defaults to the same value in every environment, and has never once been changed by an operator or a config file. It is not configuration, it is an unused parameter dressed up as flexibility.
The Abstract Base Class With Exactly One Subclass
blocks.text: The Abstract Base Class With Exactly One Subclass

blocks.content: An interface or abstract class exists, and exactly one concrete class implements it, and has for the entire history of the project. There is no second implementation planned, no test double using a different implementation, nothing. The abstraction exists purely because someone thought there might one day be a second one.
The Generic Plugin System With No Plugins
blocks.text: The Generic Plugin System With No Plugins

blocks.content: A registration mechanism, a discovery layer, and a plugin interface were built for a product that ships with exactly one built in behavior and has never had a third party or even an internal team write a second plugin. The machinery to support extension costs real maintenance, and nothing has ever used it.
More Signs to Watch For
blocks.text: More Signs to Watch For

Why These Survive Code Review
blocks.text: Why These Survive Code Review

blocks.content: None of these examples look wrong in isolation. A reviewer sees an interface and a factory and assumes good practice, not waste, because the shapes look like patterns from a textbook. The question a reviewer rarely asks out loud is the one that matters most, who else implements this, and if the honest answer is nobody, the abstraction has no job to do yet.
7. A Worked Example: The Report Exporter
blocks.text: 7. A Worked Example: The Report Exporter

blocks.content: A team is building a reporting feature for an internal dashboard. The actual requirement, confirmed by the product owner, is a single button that downloads the current table as a CSV file. Nothing else has been asked for.
Before: Speculative Flexibility
blocks.text: Before: Speculative Flexibility

blocks.content: The developer reasons that reports will probably need other formats eventually, maybe XML for a partner integration, maybe PDF for print. So instead of writing the one thing that was asked for, they build a whole exporter framework.

["Two of the three exporters throw exceptions because they were never implemented, they exist only to satisfy the interface","The ExportOptions class has five fields, and only delimiter is ever read","The factory has a single caller in the entire codebase, and it always passes \"csv\"","A new engineer reading this code assumes XML and PDF export are supported features and wastes time trying to use them"]
items: Two of the three exporters throw exceptions because they were never implemented, they exist only to satisfy the interface
The ExportOptions class has five fields, and only delimiter is ever read
The factory has a single caller in the entire codebase, and it always passes "csv"
A new engineer reading this code assumes XML and PDF export are supported features and wastes time trying to use them

blocks.content: After: Only What Today Needs
blocks.text: After: Only What Today Needs

blocks.content: The fix is not a redesign, it is a deletion. Strip the interface, the factory, the unimplemented exporters, and the unused options, and keep the one thing that is actually called.

One class, one method, no interface, no factory, no dead code paths. If XML export is ever actually requested, adding it later means adding one new class next to this one, not rewriting anything, because the existing code was never coupled to an abstraction it did not need.

blocks.title: What Changed
blocks.text: Five classes and one interface became one class. Two unimplemented methods that threw exceptions are gone. The config object with five fields nobody set became a single hardcoded delimiter, since that was the only value ever used. Nothing the product owner asked for was removed, only the parts nobody asked for.

blocks.content: How to Tell a Refactor Like This Is Safe
blocks.text: How to Tell a Refactor Like This Is Safe

blocks.content: ["Search the codebase for every call site of the interface, if there is exactly one, the interface is not doing any polymorphism work","Check whether any test exercises the unimplemented branches, if the tests only ever pass \"csv\", the other branches are untested dead code","Confirm with whoever requested the feature that no other format is on a roadmap, not \"might be,\" but confirmed","Delete first, keep the deleted code in version control, it is one revert away if it turns out to be needed"]

blocks.content: 8. When a Little Anticipatory Design Is Actually Worth It
blocks.text: 8. When a Little Anticipatory Design Is Actually Worth It

blocks.content: YAGNI does not mean never think ahead. It means do not build for a future you are only guessing at. There is a real difference between a vague someday and a near term requirement you already know is coming.
A Well Understood, Near Term Requirement
blocks.text: A Well Understood, Near Term Requirement

blocks.content: If the product roadmap, already approved, has PDF export scheduled for next sprint, and the ticket exists, that is not speculation, that is a known requirement with a delivery date. Shaping the current class so that adding the PDF path is a small, contained change is reasonable design, not a YAGNI violation. The difference between this and the plugin system built for a product with no plugins is that here the second use case is confirmed, not imagined.
Telling "Likely Next Sprint" Apart From "Maybe Someday"
blocks.text: Telling "Likely Next Sprint" Apart From "Maybe Someday"

blocks.content: A useful test is to ask who is asking for it. If a customer, a compliance requirement, or an approved roadmap item names the second use case with a rough timeframe, it is real. If the answer is "I think we might need this" with no one asking and no date attached, it is a guess, and YAGNI says wait.

["Real: a signed contract requires SSO login support shipping in Q3","Real: the security team mandates audit logging before the compliance audit next month","Guess: \"some customer might eventually want a different database\"","Guess: \"what if we go multi region someday\""]
items: Real: a signed contract requires SSO login support shipping in Q3
Real: the security team mandates audit logging before the compliance audit next month
Guess: "some customer might eventually want a different database"
Guess: "what if we go multi region someday"

blocks.content: A Small Example of Genuine Anticipatory Design
blocks.text: A Small Example of Genuine Anticipatory Design

blocks.content: Say the PDF exporter from the report example above is genuinely on the roadmap, ticketed, with a delivery date next sprint. The reasonable move is not to build the PDF exporter early, it is to shape the one method that exists so a second implementation can be added without touching call sites.

This is a one line difference from the fully simplified version, a single method interface instead of a bare class. It costs almost nothing today, and it is justified because the second implementation has a name and a date, not a maybe. Notice this is still far short of the original violation, there is still no factory, no unused options object, and no empty exporters waiting for a purpose.
The cost of being wrong about a near term, confirmed requirement is small. The cost of being wrong about a someday requirement is the entire abstraction you built for it.

9. A Self-Check Before You Add Flexibility
blocks.text: 9. A Self-Check Before You Add Flexibility

blocks.content: Before introducing an interface, a config option, a factory, or a plugin point, run through a short checklist. It takes thirty seconds and saves the maintenance cost of guessing wrong.

["Has a second concrete use case actually been requested, with a name attached, not imagined by me","If I do not build this now, how much work is it to add later, an hour, a day, or a rewrite","Am I building this because a real requirement demands it, or because it feels incomplete without it","Would I be embarrassed to explain to a teammate why this abstraction exists, given there is only one implementation","Is there a date or a name attached to the \"future need,\" or is it just \"someday\""]

The Fast Version, One Question
blocks.text: The Fast Version, One Question

blocks.content: If there is no time for the full checklist, one question captures most of it: has someone with a name and a deadline asked for this. If yes, a small amount of anticipatory design is reasonable. If the honest answer is nobody, you already have your answer, write the simple version.
10. Bringing YAGNI Back to Overengineering
blocks.text: 10. Bringing YAGNI Back to Overengineering

blocks.content: Every overengineered codebase is the sum of individual moments where someone chose to build ahead of a real need. YAGNI is what stops that sum from accumulating. It does not ask you to write worse code, it asks you to write exactly as much code as today's requirement needs, no more.

blocks.title: Two Lessons, One Discipline
blocks.content: Read together, this lesson and Overengineering vs Good Design describe the same failure from both ends. YAGNI is the check you run before you write the code. Overengineering is the name for what the codebase looks like when that check was skipped often enough. Practicing one is how you avoid the other.

The next time you catch yourself adding an interface, a config flag, or a plugin point for something that "might" be needed, stop and ask the same question this whole chapter has been circling: has anyone actually asked for this yet? If the answer is no, you already know what to do.
